message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail).
• If the landlord fails to fix, you may:
 • Withhold rent (after giving notice),
 • Pay for repairs and deduct from rent,
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Keep receipts or bank records.
• If you’re late, notify the landlord in writing and ask for a grace period if possible. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek an injunction. | | **Privacy** | • You have the right to privacy in your rented unit. | • If the landlord violates your privacy (e.g., enters without notice), you can file a complaint or seek legal action. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., breach of lease). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent (after giving notice). | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the deduction. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent increases are only allowed at the end of the lease term unless the lease allows it. | • Review the lease and state law; negotiate if necessary. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a **Notice to Pay Rent or Quit** (10 days) or **Notice to Vacate** (30 days) for non‑payment or lease violations.
• After the notice period, the landlord files a **Petition for Eviction** in court. | • Respond to the petition, attend the hearing, and present evidence. | | **Legal Assistance** | • You can seek help from:
 • Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)
 • Local tenant advocacy groups
 • Legal aid organizations (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center)
 • Private attorneys (for more complex cases). | • Contact these resources early if you face disputes. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, rent receipts, communication with the landlord, and any repair requests. 2. **Know the Timeline** – Notice periods and deadlines are strict; missing a deadline can weaken your position. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Email or certified mail provides proof of delivery. 4. **Seek Mediation First** – Many disputes can be resolved through mediation before going to court. 5. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization.
